Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 56 min read (11188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~56 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2.
  • According to recent reports, early and late H.
  • It has been revealed that establishing the environmental context of H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil3, Sangiran4 and Ngandong2 (in Java) open woodland–grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus5, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. We modelled 43 radiometric ages from five dating techniques to establish a timeline for H. erectus presence in this region. Stable and clumped isotopes and trace elements from teeth were used to establish the dominant environments and their behavioural responses. We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility. This evidence challenges the assumptions over the ecological preferences and behavioural limitations of H. erectus.

According to recent reports, early and late H. erectus finds in East and Southeast Asia represent a key part of the hominin evolutionary history of the Asian region, with China sitting in an important location to understand the dispersal, interactions and adaptations of this species6,7,8. There is a rich fossil record for H. erectus in China in Yuanmou (1.7 million years ago)9,10,11, Gongwangling (1.6 million years ago)12, Zhoukoudian (780–400 ka)13, Nanjing (approximately 650 ka)14 and Hexian (410 ka)15 (Supplementary Information 1). However, most of these sites are located in north and central China, with reliably identified and dated H. erectus fossils being conspicuously rare in southern China, especially during the Middle Pleistocene. This makes it particularly challenging to establish their ecological preferences. Furthermore, evidence of younger H. erectus (less than 400 ka) is almost entirely absent from China. This temporal gap is particularly striking given that H. erectus persisted in Java until 117–108 ka at Ngandong2, raising fundamental questions about the species’ distribution, ecological adaptations and ultimate fate in mainland China.

It has been revealed that establishing the environmental context of H. erectus is essential for understanding the species’ ecological flexibility and adaptive capabilities. The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in woodland refugia as rainforests expanded across the region, raising questions about whether encroaching closed-canopy forests contributed to the species’ eventual extinction2,16. Yet, there have been very few stable isotope studies on H. erectus evidence, as the material is often limited by diagenetic alteration3. Recent work has debated whether non-H. sapiens Middle Pleistocene hominins possessed the adaptive capabilities to exploit tropical rainforest environments17,18. Studying the forested landscapes of tropical southern China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene19 thus provides a crucial test case for assessing H. erectus ecological adaptations. Furthermore, understanding mobility patterns through techniques such as strontium isotope analysis can reveal how these populations used their landscapes and how they connected with contemporaneous populations across broader regional scales20,21.

Since the Pleistocene, tropical forest and grassland environments in southern China have provided a critical biogeographical corridor for faunal dispersals between northern latitudes and insular Southeast Asia22,23,24. The karst landscapes and cave systems of the region have yielded abundant Pleistocene faunal assemblages, yet there is presently no clear evidence that H. erectus was part of the Stegodon–Ailuropoda fauna in this region6. This raises questions as to whether the absence of H. erectus in southern China, particularly during the late Middle Pleistocene, is a consequence of ecological constraints preventing H. erectus from exploiting southern China’s tropical forest environments18, representing an effective biogeographic barrier25, or results from other factors such as an imbalance in research intensity7, a reflection of real absence of the species in the region due to alternative dispersal routes through the Tibetan corridor6, the absence of secure dating data on many out-of-context teeth, the misidentification of fragmentary remains (particularly with morphologically similar Pongo teeth26), taphonomic and preservation biases in tropical environments18, lower population densities leading to reduced fossil representation27 or the occupation of an ecological niche that is not readily preserved in cave deposits18. Distinguishing between these scenarios requires well-dated, robustly identified hominin fossils with detailed environmental context—evidence that has been lacking.

According to recent reports, to provide a temporal and environmental context for the eight H. erectus teeth6 from Baxian and Naxian caves in southern China (Fig. 1, Supplementary Information 2 and 3 and Extended Data Figs. 1–3), we used five independent dating techniques to constrain the sediments: post-infrared infrared-stimulated luminescence (pIR-IRSL) dating of feldspars, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz (Supplementary Information 4), uranium-series (U-series) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 5), coupled U-series–electron spin resonance (US-ESR) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 6) and U-series dating of carbonate capping flowstones (Supplementary Information 7), all integrated through the use of two Bayesian age models—ChronoModel and OxCal (Supplementary Information 8). Environmental reconstruction was achieved through faunal analysis (Supplementary Information 3), bulk and sequential stable isotope analysis of faunal and H. erectus tooth enamel (Supplementary Information 9) and clumped isotope thermometry of cave sediments (Supplementary Information 10). Finally, we assessed individual mobility patterns through laser-ablation trace element mapping and strontium isotope analysis of hominin tooth enamel, integrated with a regional strontium isoscape constructed using random forest machine learning to identify potential source regions (Supplementary Information 11). These multiple lines of evidence, replicated across laboratories in China and Australia, provide, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive temporal, environmental and behavioural context for late H. erectus in southern China.

a, The locations of China (green region on the world inset), Beijing (black dot) and the Chongzuo study area located in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region province, southern China (black star). b, The location of Chongzuo city in relation to Nanning and Hanoi, illustrating the dense network of karst (tan topography) that comprises this landscape. The black dashed box marks the study region and the red square represents the cave locations. The location of the lower section of Red River valley in Vietnam (discussed in the text) is marked by a red dashed line. c, Location of the Naxian and Baxian caves (red stars) connected by a 15-km karst corridor near the meandering Zuojiang River and the city of Chongzuo. Scale bars, 100 km (b), 10 km (c). Maps adapted from ref. 19, CC BY 4.0.

The Naxian and Baxian caves, located 15 km apart and situated 13 km to the northwest and 20 km to the north of Chongzuo City, respectively, are connected by a straight karst valley corridor (Fig. 1, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f and Supplementary Information 2). They are both horizontal caves at 226 and 218 m above sea level, positioned 5–7 m above the valley floor (Extended Data Fig. 2), with small fossil chambers at the rear of each cave (Fig. 2). The chambers contain remarkably similar dense, cemented, cataclastic breccias that have yielded a combined total of over 18,000 mammalian fossils, which were initially accumulated by porcupines28, including hominin remains (Supplementary Information 2). The fossil-bearing breccias (Extended Data Fig. 3) were capped by thick flowstone and underlain by younger mixed sediments (Extended Data Fig. 1d,h). This similarity suggests deposition under comparable environmental conditions.

Industry observers note that a, Cave plan for Naxian cave, showing the locations of the test pits (T1–T3) and fossil chamber at the rear of the cave. b, Expanded illustration of test pits T1 and T2 and fossil chamber in a, showing the spatial relationship between the sampling locations. c, Cross-sectional stratigraphic profile of the fossil chamber and excavation pit T2, drawn from location A–A′ in a, showing the sampling locations in the breccia, flowstone and underlying mixed unit. d,Cave plan for Baxian cave, showing the location of the two fossil chambers at the rear of the cave and the location of the test pits (T1–T3). e, Cross-sectional stratigraphic profile of the fossil chamber and excavation pit T2 drawn from location B–B′ in d, showing the sampling locations that correspond to the legend. f, Enlarged fossil chamber, showing the spatial location of the sampling in pits T2 and T3 in d. g,h, Composite stratigraphy for Naxian (g) and Baxian (h) caves, showing the sampling locations within the flowstone, breccia and underlying sandy clay. At each location, the symbols refer to the dating techniques in the legend, and the sampling codes and results have been included. Scale bars, 5 m (a), 1 m (c,e), 10 m (d).

According to recent reports, of the resulting 45 radiometric ages from both caves (Extended Data Figs. 4–7), 43 were modelled and given similar modelled age estimates (OxCal: 312–161 ka; ChronoModel: 324–184 ka at 2σ uncertainties; Extended Data Fig. 8), but the ChronoModel results were used owing to their greater outlier robustness and more reliable lower age limit. These results indicate that the age of H. erectus fossil evidence lies between 324 and 184 ka for the Baxian caves, and between 319 and 241 ka for the Naxian caves. These error limits are overlapping and broadly contemporaneous, and indicate a 95% probability that H. erectus was in this area sometime between 324 and 184 ka (see Supplementary Information 4–8 for all dating tables, data and discussion of limitations, uncertainties and choice of model; Fig. 3). The overlapping age uncertainties for the caves of approximately 78,000 years suggest a contemporaneous or near-contemporaneous presence on this landscape. The modelled ages are consistent across all five dating techniques within their respective uncertainties, providing robust constraints on the timing of H. erectus presence in this region.

a, Stratigraphy (overlying flowstone, fossil-bearing breccia and underlying clay) and modelled age range using ChronoModel (324–184 ka) of the fossil-bearing breccia for Baxian cave. The image depicts the landscape at this time, including an enclosed rainforest, H. erectus and associated fauna. b, Stratigraphy and modelled age range (319–241 ka) for the Naxian fossil-bearing breccia, along with a reconstruction of the environment around the cave at that time. The age uncertainties for the caves overlap over a period of approximately 78,000 years (green box). These reconstructions are derived from trace element and stable isotope data from the human and faunal remains seen in c and d. The dashed lines in a and b denote the age ranges for Baxian and Naxian caves, respectively, and correspond to the length of the landscape image for each cave. c, Geographic assignment based on UnionP probability surfaces calculated for three distinct 87Sr/86Sr values measured in H. erectus—(i) 0.714, (ii) 0.719 and (iii) 0.724—showing its mobility across southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The corresponding strontium isoscape and full method are provided in Supplementary Information 11. d, Biplots of δ13Ccarbon source and δ18O values by taxon in relation to vegetation type. Biplot of faunal enamel δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ Vienna Peedee Belemnite standard (VPDB)) and δ18O (‰ VPDB) at Baxian (top; 324–184 ka) and Naxian (bottom; 319–241 ka) caves. Each taxon is represented by a unique combination of colour and shape. Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense-canopy forest (green shading), C3 vegetation (light green shading) and C4 grassland (yellow shading). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense-canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. Scale bars, 50 km (c). Bax, Baxian; Nax, Naxian.

The faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

In a recent development, the plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

According to recent reports, independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

Recent findings suggest that three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and at the moment restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

Recent findings suggest that high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave showed overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

In a recent development, A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

Geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

It has been revealed that the temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

Moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

Industry observers note that areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

Recent findings suggest that our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

The caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

Industry observers note that the fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

According to recent reports, measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Sources indicate that seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a New Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

In a recent development, one H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

Separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

In a recent development, two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

According to recent reports, three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

According to recent reports, three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

One H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning were based on the global bioavailable strontium database in ref. 33 and all R scripts necessary for generating isoscapes are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21131183)74.

It has been revealed that a-d Naxian cave, a and b the cave – location marked with a red star - is situated on the outer cone of a karst inselberg located close to a highway. c a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology of the cave with the small entrance and flowstone step that leads into the stalagmite chamber dense with speleothem, a larger chamber with narrow and high ceilings and terminating with a small fossil chamber with breccia, d the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain by a younger underlying mixed material below. e-h Baxian Cave e and f the cave is also situated on the outer edge of a karst cone with the limestone corridor than connects both caves, cave location is marked with a red star, g a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology and sedimentology of the cave from the wide and high entrance to the narrower and smaller passage that lead to the confined fossil chamber, h the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain with the younger underlying mixed material. There is a remarkable similarity between the stratigraphy and sedimentology of these deposits and associated fossils (d, h).

The images of the fossil chambers are taken from a 3D models of the caves (Supplementary Information 2 for links).

a: Combined p-value (physical uranium uptake parameter) trajectories for enamel and dentine illustrating the relative goodness-of-fit of uranium-uptake histories over the modelled time interval. The enamel curve highlights a broader temporal sensitivity, while dentine exhibits steeper p-value responses reflecting higher susceptibility to uranium migration. b: Normalised uranium-uptake curves for enamel (red) and dentine (green) showing contrasting U-uptake kinetics, with enamel characterised by delayed uptake and dentine by more rapid early incorporation. c: Frequency distribution of modelled ages generated under the US-ESR age model, illustrating the central tendency and dispersion of the Monte-Carlo age simulations used to derive the final age estimate, d H. erectus tooth from Baxian that was dated using US-ESR techniques (Supplementary Information 6).

Industry observers note that a and b are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr for the five dating techniques modelled according to Oxcal and applied to the sediments and fossils of Naxian (a) and Baxian (b) caves. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The techniques are colour coded according to the legend and organised into the unit in which they were sampled from – the flowstone, breccia or underlying clay. Some of the techniques represent minimum ages (such as the US ages on teeth) and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the right, while other represent maximum ages such as the pIR-IRSL single aliquot dating of feldspars and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the left. The thick black horizontal boxes with dashed lines represent the boundary ages (and errors) estimated by the modelling. The boundary ages quoted represent the upper and lower age ranges for the breccia units in both caves. c and d are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr modelling according to Chronomodel for the same five dating techniques. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The individual sample events have been organised into three phases; breccia deposition (including fossil and sediment ages), overlying flowstone precipitation and underlying clay deposition with each phase represented by a different plot. The timescale goes from more recent on the right (50 ka written as -50000) to oldest on the left (400 ka written as -400000). For Baxian (c) we have used the age uncertainty at 2 σ (95%) of the fossil teeth dated using US-ESR (H. erectus and Pongo), resulting in an age of 324-184 ka. For Naxian (d), the fossils are all dated using US only so represent minimum ages, so instead we have used the period between the overlying flowstone (as the minimum age) and the youngest soda straw in the breccia (as the maximum age) both at 2 σ (95%) uncertainty to constrain the age of breccia deposition at 319-241 ka. The use of Chronomodel compared to Oxcal has accentuated similar events and reduced the younger age uncertainty by around 20 kyr. The overlapping uncertainty between the two caves has been used to represent a Homo erectus presence at some point between 324-184 ka.

It has been revealed that a Taxon-specific δ13Ccarbon source values in relation to vegetation type. δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ VPDB at Baxian (324-184) and Naxian (319-241 ka). Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense canopy forest (dark green), C3 vegetation (light green), and C4 grassland (yellow). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. The H. erectus values (red stars) fall within the C3 forest domain and plot at the boundary between dense canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. b Vegetation zone proportions at hominin-bearing sites in Southeast Asia and South China. Proportional distribution of faunal δ13Ccarbon source values assigned to vegetation zones (dense canopy C3, open C3, C3–C4 intermediate, and C4). Bars show the relative contributions of each zone across six hominin-bearing sites: Trinil4, Sangiran5, Cobra Cave34,73, Duoi U’Oi74, Lida Ajer45,75, Baxian and Naxian. Baxian and Naxian are dominated by C3 signals, with substantial contributions from dense canopy vegetation, while Trinil and Sangiran show higher proportions of intermediate and C4 values, reflecting more open habitats. Lida Ajer is strongly weighted toward dense canopy values, consistent with closed rainforest settings. Together, these results illustrate marked ecological contrasts between late H. erectus contexts in China and Javanese sites, as well as affinities between Naxian and the rainforest environment of early H. sapiens at Lida Ajer75,76,77.

a Trace element distribution maps of the Baxian H. erectus tooth. LA-ICP-MS elemental maps showing the distribution of (i) 7Li/43Ca, (ii) 88Sr/43Ca, (iii) 138Ba/43Ca, and (iv) 238U/43Ca ratios normalised to calcium across a longitudinal section of the tooth. All maps show both enamel (upper/left portion, blue-green colours) and dentine (lower/right portion, predominantly dark red). The colour scales are optimised to visualise variation within the enamel tissue. Dark red areas in the dentine for Sr, Ba, and U maps indicate significantly elevated concentrations due to post-depositional diagenetic uptake from the burial environment, rendering these tissues unsuitable for life history reconstruction. In contrast, the enamel tissue displays lower concentrations and visible banding patterns, particularly Ba/Ca, and Sr/Ca maps, which reflect biogenic signals. The U/Ca map clearly illustrates the extent of diagenetic alteration, with the highest concentrations in dentine and at the enamel-dentine junction (EDJ), demonstrating the vulnerability of dental tissues to post-depositional elemental exchange. The Li/Ca map shows elevated concentrations in both tissues with distinct banding in the enamel. All measurements were obtained using LA-ICP-MS with 40 μm spot size and Ca-normalization to account for matrix effects. b Strontium isotope ratio profiles across H. erectus tooth enamel from Baxian and Naxian caves. LA-MC-ICP-MS 87Sr/86Sr ratio profiles measured along linear transects across tooth enamel from (i) BAX-1 from Baxian Cave, and (ii) NX-A1, (iii) NX-B1, and (iv) NX-B2 from Naxian Cave. The x-axis represents distance in mm along the ablation transect from the cervical region toward the cusp, corresponding to the temporal sequence of enamel formation from early to late childhood. The y-axis shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with variation reflecting changes in geological substrate accessed through diet and drinking water during tooth formation. All four individuals exhibit substantial intra-tooth variation in 87Sr/86Sr ratios that exceeds analytical uncertainty, indicating mobility between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood. BAX-1 shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220, while the Naxian specimens display overlapping ranges: NX-A1 (0.7115-0.7165), NX-B1 (0.7095-0.7165), and NX-B2 (0.7100-0.7160). The observed variation patterns provide evidence for landscape mobility of late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus populations in southern China. c Strontium isoscape and geographic assignment probabilities for H. erectus mobility in southern China and northern Southeast Asia. (i) Regional-scale strontium isoscape showing predicted bioavailable 87Sr/86Sr ratios across southern China, northern Vietnam, northern Laos, and adjacent regions. Colours indicate 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.710 (dark blue) to 0.725 (pink), with the Baxian/Naxian cave sites marked by a white dot. Major cities (Hanoi, Lào Cai, Guilin) are shown for geographic reference. (ii) Prediction uncertainty map for the regional isoscape, showing standard error of predicted 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.004 (yellow, low uncertainty) to 0.016 (purple, high uncertainty). (iii) Local-scale isoscape focused on a 400 km × 400 km region centred on the Baxian/Naxian sites, with scale bar representing 50 km. (iv) Prediction uncertainty map for the local isoscape (v-vii) Geographic assignment probability maps for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in H. erectus tooth enamel: (v) Seq1 = 0.714, representing average values for NX-A1 and lower values in NX-B2, showing high assignment probabilities (yellow-green) concentrated within 30-50 km of the cave sites in limestone karst terrain; (vi) Seq2 = 0.719, representing transitional values observed in multiple specimens, showing assignment probabilities extending southward ~150-250 km toward the Red River valley region; (vii) Seq3 = 0.724, representing the most radiogenic values observed (particularly in BAX-1), showing assignment probabilities concentrated in the Red River valley foothills approximately 250 km south of the caves and near Lào Cai to the west, with very low probabilities in the local cave area (dark purple). The progressive southward shift in assignment probabilities from Seq1 to Seq3 indicates long-distance mobility of late H. erectus individuals between the local karst uplands and distant regions up to 250 km away during childhood tooth formation. All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning based on33 global bioavailable strontium database.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing footballer Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.
  • Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates' Court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the opening match of the Premier League season at Anfield on August 15 last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 05:49 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 08:12 EST, 20 November 2026.

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing footballer Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates' Court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the opening match of the Premier League season at Anfield on August 15 last year.

But Simon Jones, prosecuting, said: 'Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him.

'In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case.' District Judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.

Semenyo, who was a Bournemouth player at the time of the incident but later signed for Manchester City, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mr Mogan was taken to hospital after suffering a seizure.

The court had heard Mr Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game.

Mark Mogan (right) has been found not guilty of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo (left) after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

He was alleged to have said: 'Hurry up and take the throw-in, you black b*****d.'.

Opening the case last month, Mr Jones said: 'That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him.

'Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn't believe what the male had said.' Mr Mogan then shouted "I'm talking to you, you ****", the court heard.

Witnesses also said they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.

Semenyo reported the incident to the match referee and Mr Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time.

Mr Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to 'hurry up'.

Mr Mogan, of Templehill Close in Dovecot, Liverpool, declined to comment as he left court.

Semenyo, who scored a brace in the game, had brought the incident to the attention of match referee Anthony Taylor and the match was briefly halted while both managers and captains were spoken to.

At half time an announcement was made to the crowd asking for no racist abuse and pictures on social media showed a man in a wheelchair being escorted along the touchline and out of the ground.

Mogan, pictured with Liverpool legend Robbie Fowler, would have been banned for life if he'd have been found guilty.

Merseyside Police later announced the man had been arrested and then was bailed for three months pending further investigations.

Pictures on social media showed Mogan playing wheelchair basketball for a team called the Greenbank Meteors while other images show him posing with Liverpool legends Robbie Fowler and Emile Heskey.

After he was charged, Liverpool confirmed he would be banned for life if found guilty but Judge Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty on Friday morning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crystal Palace defender Oscar Mingueza is a doubt for Thursday’s Europa League clash with Real Sociedad after missing out through injury against Coventry.

Mingueza was absent from the squad that travelled to Coventry for Thomas Frank’s first game in charge of Palace, and Standard Sport understands that the Spanish full-back has suffered an adductor overload.

The 27-year-old, who arrived at Palace on a free transfer over the summer, has been for a scan, and while his injury is not believed to be serious, it is unclear whether he will be fit to face Real Sociedad at Selhurst Park on Thursday evening.

Mingueza has played nine games in all competitions for Palace this season, but has started just twice in the Premier League, with fellow summer signing Anan Khalaili preferred on the right-hand side of defence.

Speaking about Mingueza’s injury before kick-off against Coventry, Frank said he was hopeful that he could be available against Sociedad.

“Oscar Mingueza unfortunately picked up the smallest of knocks, keeping him out of this game. But we’re hopeful for Thursday,” Frank mentioned.

Palace tasted defeat in their first game under Frank as Dwight McNeil’s 85th-minute own-goal handed Coventry a 3-2 win at the CBS Arena.

They remain rooted to the bottom of the Premier League table, having won two of their opening 11 league games.

Bayern Munich’s supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge has suggested Jamal Musiala may be offered a pay cut due to his health situation and claims no club would buy the midfielder ‘under these conditions’.

The 23-year-old collapsed in two different games in the space of four days during Bayern’s pre-season campaign in the summer.

Musiala later revealed that he had been suffering from ‘brief, temporary – but treatable – absence seizures resulting from a neurological dysfunction’.

The midfielder also suffered a thigh injury in September and made his return from his two-month absence on Friday night as Bayern drew 1-1 with FC Koln.

Speaking after the game, Rummenigge insisted Bayern must consider their financial situation with Musiala on a contract which is worth in excess of €25 million (£20.9m) a year and expires in 2030.

‘What we know unfortunately suggests that it will be difficult to reach the level he has so often shown here in the stadium,’ Rummenigge told Sky Germany.

‘We need to talk to the family, the player, and the agency, because then these sums of money, sorry, with all due respect, are no longer feasible.

‘I cannot imagine that Jamal wants to leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions.

‘We are all interested in his return, ideally in top form. But what happens if that isn’t the case? Then we still have to think about the finances.

‘The discussion hasn’t taken place yet. These are just ideas at this stage.’.

Speaking earlier this month, Bayern’s honorary president, Uli Hoeness, also raised questions about Musiala’s contract due to his health matter.

‘We are facing a dilemma in this case, as he is suffering from an illness that cannot simply be cured, but it can be controlled to a certain extent with the use of medication,’ Hoeness remarked.

‘But whether he ​will have the same performance potential that he had… imagine if Bayern were now to question ‌his ⁠contract and say that what he is capable of delivering now is no longer what is in the contract.’.

When asked about the assessment of Musiala’s by the club’s hierarchy, Bayern head coach Vincent Kompany remarked: ‘I have a very clear role in this club, as a coach, I have to believe in my players and that we can achieve something together.

‘If Jamal finds his level and form again, and we manage to do that together, then everyone wins – Bayern, the fans, and I believe German football as a whole. Because Jamal is a special player.

According to recent reports, ‘That is my role, quite clearly. If a coach does something different or claims something different, then there is a problem, in my opinion.’.

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

According to recent reports, “I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old remarked. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”.

The Frenchman remarked that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

According to recent reports, “I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

Industry observers note that “Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”.

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he mentioned. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”.

It has been revealed that for all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Sources indicate that “The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage noted. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”.

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Industry observers note that brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

It has been revealed that yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German remarked: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”.

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

Xabi Alonso had been clear that he wanted his Chelsea team to match Leeds physically and mentally in the spirit of this historically feisty fixture.

What he got in the end, though, was yet more evidence that this young team are there for the taking by those who want to take the game to them.

Leeds were sharper and nastier in every aspect today, and while Chelsea took the lead through Emmanuel Emegha, it came as no surprise to see Daniel Farke’s men snap back to equalise before running away with the game with such ferocity that Alonso’s future will, for the first time, come under some scrutiny.

There were boos at the break with the score level, but Leeds firmly on top, and the shower of condemnation that followed the full-time whistle vocalised in the clearest terms that Alonso is under pressure.

Alonso’s Blues started the season ferociously and looked like they could challenge for major honours, but Chelsea supporters have been here before.

They were always going to need more than a few exhilarating attacking displays to nail their names to the mast of a title challenge, and so it has proved.

Leeds dominated both boxes and were first to every ball, bullying Chelsea’s defence just as Sunderland and Brian Brobbey had before the international break.

Lessons have not been learned from last week, from last season or, frankly, any point of the BlueCo ownership. Chelsea as a team, while not short on quality, remain short of leaders.

In a recent development, they have looked to shoehorn young men into positions of responsibility, and this is the inevitable result. Teams with nous, experience and bite will continue to see Stamford Bridge as a challenge they can scale.

This was Leeds’ first win in this corner of west London since the turn of the millennium, the latest in a long list of teams to head to a formerly impenetrable Stamford Bridge and make history.

According to recent reports, chelsea rarely have answers for teams who seek to raise the temperature of the game. When the game becomes stretched, Chelsea become increasingly erratic and tempestuous.

Recent findings suggest that it is in these moments that the typically composed Alonso must do more to change the tide. His changes this afternoon came too late and made no difference. Leeds were in control of the game and the scoreline when Alonso turned to his bench just past the hour mark.

Cole Palmer was involved in an angry exchange with Joao Pedro after the final whistle of Chelsea’s woeful home defeat to Leeds United.

Xabi Alonso’s side were thrashed 4-1 at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon with the visitors scoring three times in the second-half to seal a famous win in the capital.

Emmanuel Emegha opened the scoring for the hosts after 25 minutes before Noah Okafor levelled the contest three minutes later.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin put Leeds back in front eight minutes into the second-half before Okafor added his second of the afternoon.

Brenden Aaronson wrapped things up with a fine solo effort in added time to seal win that moved Leeds ahead of Chelsea in the Premier League table.

Pedro was not in the squad, still recovering from a thigh injury that has now ruled him out of Chelsea’s last five games.

It had been hoped he would be fit after the international break but Xabi Alonso revealed on Friday the striker was still not back in training.

The Brazil international was in attendance on Saturday afternoon and was involved in a tense exchange with one of his teammates immediately after the game.

https://t.co/XbtQBfLgcq pic.twitter.com/O7XJbYIay6.

The Athletic report Palmer appeared to have an angry exchange of words with Pedro as he left the pitch.

Industry observers note that in footage shared on social media, Palmer is seen approaching his teammate, covering his mouth with his hand as he speaks. Pedro puts his arms on his teammate’s shoulders, shrugging his shoulders in response as Palmer walks away unhappy.

During Alonso’s post-match press conference, one journalist suggested the disagreement was sparked when Pedro tried to get Palmer to go and applaud the fans with the England international seemingly reluctant.

Alonso said of the incident: ‘No, we were disappointed, the fans were disappointed because the expectations from them are high and we feel sorry for them and we need to go through together and to find solutions to that and now, as I said, for sure it’s not the easiest moment.

‘It’s a fragile moment but we need to work together and stick together because there is still so long way to go..

Palmer had played the full 90 minutes but was unable to inspire his side who have now won just one of their last five games.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Jonathan O'Shea | 21 Nov 2026 09:32.
  • Both battling at the wrong end of the Serie A standings, Monza and Fiorentina will vie for three precious points when matchday 12 comes to a close on Monday night.
  • While the hosts have slumped into the drop zone after four consecutive defeats, their Viola visitors are showing signs of revival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 21 Nov 2026 09:32.

Both battling at the wrong end of the Serie A standings, Monza and Fiorentina will vie for three precious points when matchday 12 comes to a close on Monday night.

While the hosts have slumped into the drop zone after four consecutive defeats, their Viola visitors are showing signs of revival.

Having lost six of their first eight games and recalled their former interim manager, Fiorentina had begun to steady the ship before international football intervened.

Paolo Vanoli's side have inched away from the relegation zone by claiming five points from their last three outings, with an away victory over Sassuolo being sandwiched by a pair of 2-2 home draws.

After sharing the spoils with Atalanta at the end of October, the Viola fought hard for a draw against old foes Juventus, taking the lead twice before settling for one point.

Both acceptable results in isolation, but Fiorentina's struggles at Stadio Franchi show no sign of ending: the Tuscan club's last league win on home turf dates back to April.

Now bound for Brianza, their two top-flight wins this term have both come on the road, so they will hope to pick up another on Monday.

However, sitting just two points above Monza, Fiorentina have yet to keep a clean sheet in Serie A and continue to look vulnerable at the back.

Across seven prior meetings in Monza, there have been three wins apiece, but the hosts have won two of the last three.

While precedent may suggest that they will come out on top, the Brianzoli departed for the international break on a dismal run of form.

Consecutive defeats to Torino, Napoli, Bologna and Atalanta left them stuck inside the drop zone, abruptly halting a relatively promising start.

Only Sassuolo have conceded more goals after 11 matchdays, leaving head coach Ivan Juric searching for solutions to his team's defensive woes.

Failing to score for the first time this season, the Serie B playoff winners were beaten 1-0 by La Dea last time out, continuing a grim top-flight record at Stadio Brianteo.

Dating back to their relegation campaign of 2024-25, Monza have won just three of their last 24 home games in Serie A.

Although expensive summer signing Arthur Atta is set to end a six-match absence, Fiorentina are still missing Fabiano Parisi and Marin Pongracic due to injury.

Alieu Njie returned from Sweden duty with a minor thigh problem, so Wilfried Gnonto or Pedro Goncalves could be promoted from the bench if required.

As part of an attacking trio, Njie has racked up five goal involvements from his last three Serie A appearances, while Argentine pair Mateo Pellegrino and Franco Mastantuono both have four goals this season.

Meanwhile, one man has been carrying Monza's attack: Capocannoniere leader and Liverpool target Gustavo Varela has scored more than half of their 17 league goals, netting nine in 10 games.

In the three-points-for-a-win era, only Fiorentina legend Gabriel Batistuta (13) and David Trezeguet of Juventus (10) have topped his tally for a newly promoted side after 11 matchdays.

Monza captain Matteo Pessina returned to full training during the break, having missed most of the campaign so far.

Former Fiorentina midfielder Michael Folorunsho has also recovered from a calf problem, but Yvan Maye and Jay Robinson are both doubts.

Monza possible starting lineup:.

Tornqvist; Kouadio, Goglichidze, Lucchesi; Birindelli, Akinsanmiro, Foe Ondoa, Mangas; Mota, Robinson; Varela.

Fiorentina possible starting lineup:.

De Gea; Jimenez, Dragusin, Viery, Mario; Ndour, Fagioli, Oulai; Mastantuono, Pellegrino, Gnonto.

Fiorentina have equalled their worst defensive start to any Serie A season -  a negative record set back in 1933 - while Monza have never conceded more at this stage of a top-flight campaign.

They will surely share several goals on Monday night, but the Viola's vibrant attack should secure maximum points.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glenn Murray believes Bruno Fernandes will look to leave the club if he doesn’t sign a upcoming Manchester United contract before the January transfer window.

Fernandes won the PFA Players’ Player of the Year last year after a superb second half of the season under Michael Carrick, but has not hit those same heights so far this campaign.

The Red Devils captain was also dropped for a game after publicly criticising Carrick’s tactics following a heavy Champions League defeat to Como.

The arrival of Mauricio Pochettino represents a fresh start for Fernandes this season, but there remains uncertainty over his long-term future at the club given the 32-year-old is out of contract at the end of the season.

Fernandes has already turned down two contract offers from the club, and former Brighton striker Murray believes he could be eyeing up a move away from Old Trafford when the transfer window reopens in January.

‘I wouldn’t burst the bank [on a upcoming contract] for him,’ Murray told Sky Sports. ‘I think he’s not the future of the football club.

‘Listen, he’s given his best years to Manchester United and unfortunately they haven’t won an awful lot, which he would have liked.

‘I think if he gets the option to move on, and it gets to January, and he can start speaking to other people, I think it will open his eyes up to see where he could go and if he could win things and finish off his career more enjoyably, because there have been years at Manchester United that have been really difficult.

‘He has been the standout player, but he is not the future and it could be time to part ways.

‘It all depends on the salary because if you outlay a lot [on wages], there is nothing coming back on the other end at this point of his career.’.

Pochettino, meanwhile, has confirmed that Fernandes will remain captain under his management and insisted the midfielder is an ‘crucial’ player for his rebuild.

‘All the players, we were chatting, it was amazing from day one, Bruno is our captain, an key player,’ Pochettino confirmed.

‘But all the players need to think they are important, from the bottom to the top.

‘I spent three hours, chatting in my office, with all the players, maybe I miss some injured players. In the next few days, we will talk in an individual way with all of them.

‘It’s important to listen to what they need to say, understand the place they are. Not only on the field, off the field, what’s going on. Some conversations, some collective way, meetings, but focus is on Sunday.’.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin believes Chelsea’s players could not handle the ‘intensity’ during Leeds United’s 4-1 win at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Chelsea took the lead in the first half through an excellent finish from Emmanuel Emegha but Xabi Alonso’s side were in front for just three minutes as Noah Okafor pulled Leeds level.

Leeds then came out flying in the second half and Leeds were given a penalty after Jayden Bogle’s thumping strike hit Rogers on the top of his arm.

Calvert-Lewin converted the spot-kick to put Leeds ahead and Daniel Farke’s side continued their dominance in the second half as Okafor netted his second of the game before Brenden Aaronson completed the deserved victory with a goal in injury time.

Chelsea have now been beaten in three out of their last four Premier League games, while only Coventry City, Ipswich Town and Crystal Palace have conceded more goals than Xabi Alonso’s side this season.

During his post-match interview with Sky Sports, Calvert-Lewin was asked what the message was from Farke during the half-time break with Chelsea already showing signs of fragility.

‘The message was just more of the same. I think we were going well, we just weren’t putting our chances away and we knew the next chance was coming and we’d have to take it,’ Calvert-Lewin replied.

‘To be honest, I expected Chelsea to come out with a bit more oomph in the second half but I think our intensity, the way that we played and the way we set up against them, they couldn’t handle it, and I think that reflected in the scoreline.’.

Asked what the message was ahead of the game against Chelsea, Calvert-Lewin replied: ‘Intensity, bring the intensity from the start.

Diego Simeone has called for perspective amid concerns over the form of Atletico Madrid's strikers, insisting he is "excited" by his side's progress despite their lack of goals.

Ahead of Sunday's Madrid derby against Getafe at the Estadio Coliseum, Simeone reiterated his confidence in his forwards, pointing to the contributions of Atletico's other attacking players as a reason for optimism.

Indeed, Julian Alvarez, Jonathan David and Alexander Sorloth have combined for just four LaLiga goals between them this season, leaving much of the goalscoring burden on Atletico's wide players, with Alex Baena (five goals), Giuliano Simeone (four) and Alejandro Grimaldo (four) leading the way.

Despite their strikers' struggles, Atletico sit third in LaLiga, five points behind second-placed Real Madrid and leaders Barcelona.

"On the goals, it's all about perspective," Simeone remarked. "I'm excited that we're where we are without the strikers scoring.

"Hopefully, the goals will come, and then we can build on all the good things we're doing.

"We're going to face Getafe, who are a very tough opponent on their home turf. We need to play a strong game and take the match to where we can hurt them.

"We need to maintain what we've been doing and continue managing our playing time so that we can show our ability to compete at the level we need to.".

The Atletico boss also provided updates on defenders Robin Le Normand and Cristian Romero, both of whom have featured regularly for Atletico this season.

"We have a lot of confidence in [Le Normand]," Simeone added.

"We have a very good relationship, we often talk about what's been happening to him. In football, mistakes are more damaging to defenders, but with his personality he'll do well.

It has been revealed that "Cuti Romero also is working very hard to recover as quickly as possible. Even without playing, he's very important. We need the best Cuti Romero.".

Getafe, meanwhile, are 15th ahead of Sunday's kick-off, though Jose Bordalas' side remain unbeaten at home in the league this season (W3 D3), and have not suffered defeat across their last eight LaLiga matches.

— Atlético de Madrid (@atletienglish) November 21, 2026.

Enes Unal has scored five goals in 12 games against Atletico in LaLiga – his highest tally against a single opponent in the top-flight.

Lee Kang-In has found the net three times in eight LaLiga outings against Getafe.

Against no other opponent has he scored more goals across his career in Europe's top five leagues, along with three against Angers for Paris Saint-Germain in Ligue 1.

MATCH PREDICTION: ATLETICO MADRID WIN.

Atletico head into this clash as favourites, having won 10 of their 13 away matches against Getafe in LaLiga (D2 L1).

Los Colchoneros have not managed more away wins against any other opponent in the league (also 10 against Celta Vigo).

According to recent reports, simeone's side also arrive in strong away form, having won their last four LaLiga matches on the road. They have only managed five or more consecutive away victories in a single campaign on two previous occasions – in April 2014 and February 2021, both of which were title-winning seasons.

Recent findings suggest that simeone himself boasts an impressive record against Getafe, having won 22 of his 27 LaLiga meetings with them (D4 L1). Victory on Sunday would see him equal Luis Aragones' record for the most wins by a manager against a single opponent in the competition, with the latter having beaten Espanyol 23 times.

Getafe, though, have taken points from three of their last seven league meetings with Atleti (W1 D2 L4), having done so in just two of the previous 20 (D2 L18).

Bordalas' side will also take confidence from their recent form at the Coliseum, where they are unbeaten in eight LaLiga matches (W5 D3) – their longest such run since going 11 games without defeat between May and December 2023 (W7 D4).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xabi Alonso has provided an upgrade on Moises Caicedo after the midfielder was forced off in the first-half of Chelsea’s 4-1 defeat to Leeds United.

The Blues fell to a dismal defeat at home on Saturday afternoon with Leeds scoring three times in the second-half to seal a famous win in west London.

Caicedo started for the hosts having asked to come off at half-time playing for Ecuador on Tuesday against Bolivia, later explaining he ‘didn’t feel very well’.

During an aerial dual with James Justin in the first-half at Stamford Bridge, the midfielder suffered a heavy landing after twisting in mid-air.

While he was initially able to carry on, Caicedo went down again off the ball a few minutes later, covering his face with his shirt in disappointment.

In a recent development, he was replaced after just 22 minutes with Jordan Henderson onto replace him. Caicedo did not go straight down the tunnel and instead watched the action from the bench with an ice pack.

Asked for an update after the game, Alonso explained the former Brighton star was in ‘pain’ and would require further assessment.

‘He has a knock and we need to wait until tomorrow to see how he is,’ Alonso mentioned in his post-match press conference.

‘He was in pain and let’s see how bad it is.’.

Chelsea are already without a number of key players. Joao Pedro and Maxence Lacroix were absent again against Leeds, still recovering from respective thigh and hamstring complications with Alonso unable to out a timeframe on their returns when he spoke to the media on Friday.

Reece James meanwhile is also still absent as he recovers from minor knee surgery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frosinone forward Romano Schmid believes that his side will have to be more ‘proactive’ in order to get a positive result against AC Milan.

Having been promoted from Serie B last season, Frosinone have been the surprise package so far in Serie A barring perhaps the league-leaders Lazio, as they sit sixth in the table having won six of their opening 11 games so far.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

They were heavily tipped to be in a relegation battle by pundits and the bookmakers, and yet they have scored 24 goals and allowed just 15, making them not just an effective team but also an entertaining one too.

Sources indicate that the summer arrival Schmid – who signed from Werder Bremen – has been a part of that. He spoke at a press conference two days before Frosinone’s trip north to face Milan at San Siro. The questions and his responses were relayed by TuttoFrosinone.

After Cagliari, what will the match against Milan be like?

It has been revealed that “The match in Milan will be completely different from the one in Cagliari. Milan are obviously the favourites, their game is different from Cagliari’s, and we’ll need a more proactive Frosinone.”.

How are you finding Serie A as a league?

According to recent reports, “It’s different from the Bundesliga, I like it. You have to always be on top of things otherwise you lose the duels, especially in midfield.”.

Did the fact that they play with a 4-2-3-1 like with Austria influence your choice to come to Frosinone?

“It’s not the main reason. With the national team, we don’t play man-to-man like here against Frosinone. It’s a similar game because we definitely play deep, we attack high.”.

Why did you miss Austria’s last match?

“My son had a problem, it wasn’t serious but he wasn’t feeling very well and since we had already qualified I preferred to stay with the family”.

You are one of the most important signings in Frosinone’s history, and it’s no coincidence that you started playing immediately under Alvini. How do you feel?

“My past performances in the Bundesliga were crucial; that’s one of the reasons Froisnone chose me, given my previous performances. They’re similar to what I played under coach Alvini. I’m enjoying myself and I’m happy.”.

Where do you prefer to play, in the attacking midfield role or in the pivot?

Sources indicate that “My favourite position is number 10, an attacking midfielder behind the centre-forward. I feel comfortable playing there, I’ve also tried playing further back, but my favourite position is still number 10.”.

According to recent reports, “I haven’t played PlayStation for the last 4-5 years, since I became a father. Last night my wife downloaded the game and we played together.”.
